title: Joined or spaced
hook: a hashtag with no spaces gets misread; older copies of the Granth run every word together
tomorrow: what's the line of small print above every hymn?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tippi: a small curved mark that adds a hum, the n in sangat and in Granth. Small marks matter. Today, the smallest mark of all: a space.
screen: `TIPPI: SMALL MARKS MATTER.` → `THE SMALLEST MARK: A SPACE.`

segments.voice: A hashtag with no spaces can be read two ways, and somebody always reads it the wrong way. Now try a whole page like that. In older hand-written copies of the Granth, the words run on, letter after letter, line after line, with no gaps. That's called larivaar. Many printed copies today put a space between each word; that's called padched. Same letters, different page. And in a gurdwara, the copy on the high seat may well be the joined one. So which should a reader learn on?
screen: `A HASHTAG, READ WRONG.` → `LARIVAAR: THE WORDS JOINED.` → `PADCHED: THE WORDS SPACED.` → `WHICH TO LEARN ON?`

segments.voice: Two real views, each in its own best words. First, the case for larivaar. This is the Granth as it was written and handed down, and there's respect in leaving it whole. Because the words aren't broken for you, you have to learn where they break, slowly, usually with a teacher. That slowness is the point. It keeps a reader close to every line, and it keeps any one editor's word breaks from quietly becoming the only reading. Now the case for padched. The letters are exactly the same; nothing is added but space. And space opens the page to anyone who can read Gurmukhi, at home, on a phone, with no teacher nearby. Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase, that the teaching is shared by everyone, people of every class alike. A spaced page puts that sharing into practice. Some families keep both: a larivaar copy where the Guru is formally seated, a spaced gutka or app for every day. Neither side wants the words changed. Neither wants them rushed. And here's what they share, which is today's line: whichever copy is open, the Guru's words are read word by word. Run them together carelessly and a line can blur into something it never said. Take them one at a time and they land.
screen: `FOR LARIVAAR: LEARN WHERE WORDS BREAK.` · `FOR PADCHED: THE SAME LETTERS, OPEN.` · `SOME KEEP BOTH.` · `EITHER WAY, ONE WORD AT A TIME.` · then, large: `WORD BY WORD.`

segments.voice: Choose one short line, from the Japji or any page you have. Say it out loud slowly, one word on each breath out, with a full pause between the words. If your copy is spaced, let the gaps set the pace; if it's joined, let your breath find the breaks.
Larivaar: a copy of the Granth with the words written joined, no spaces between them, as in older hand-written copies. The fifth word of the year.
Your line: word by word. Joined or spaced, that's how the Guru's words are read. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1431 COUNTS.` → `READING THE GRANTH · 5 OF 20.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT'S THE LINE OF SMALL PRINT ABOVE EVERY HYMN?`

howItsDone: Some gurdwaras seat a larivaar copy of the Guru Granth Sahib for the main reading, and readers learn its word breaks through santhiaa with a teacher; many Sikhs read daily from spaced (padched) gutkas, printed copies or apps.

chat.meaning: Larivaar keeps the text joined and asks for slow, taught reading; padched opens the same letters to more readers. Either way, word by word.
